title: The wind and the rock (7–14)
hookLine: Mara overthrows the careless like wind a weak tree, not the steady; rain gets through a badly thatched roof

cards: After a big storm, walk through a neighborhood and look at what came down. Often it isn't the tallest tree. It's the one that was already hollow, or shallow-rooted, or leaning.
The old oak at the corner is still standing; the young tree with no roots is across the road.
Inside the houses, the leaks show up exactly where the roof was already weak: the missing shingle, the cracked flashing you meant to fix in the summer. Storms don't make weak spots. They find them.

teach.b: Verse seven describes someone living for pleasure only, senses unguarded, eating without limit, idle and weak.
And Mara, the tempter, the figure who stands for everything that pulls people off the path, “will certainly overthrow him, as the wind throws down a weak tree.”
Verse eight is the twin: the one who lives with guarded senses, moderate in food, faithful and strong, Mara can no more throw down “than the wind throws down a rocky mountain.” Wind and rock.
The wind is the same for both. What differs is what it meets. Verses nine to twelve warn against wearing the robe without the inner change, and against mistaking what's false for what's true.
Then thirteen and fourteen: “As rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, passion will break through an unreflecting mind.”

And the twin: “As rain does not break through a well-thatched house, passion will not break through a well-reflecting mind.” The commentary tells these verses about Nanda, the Buddha's own half-brother.
He became a monk on the day of his wedding, almost without meaning to, and pined for the bride he'd left behind.
His roof leaked everywhere. But with patience and practice, the story says, he thatched it, and became known for guarding his senses. Thatching isn't done once.
You check it before the rains, replace a bundle here, tie down a corner there. Not an unbreakable fortress: a roof kept in repair.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the thatched-roof verses to explain guarding the senses and steady daily practice: small, repeated repairs rather than one great effort.

o: badly thatched, so the rain gets through the roof
a roof torn off completely by a heavy storm
a house left empty when its owner goes away

games.q: match the pictures in verses seven to fourteen.
p: the careless, thrown down by the wind
the half-brother who thatched his roof

s: in these verses the wind is stronger for some people than for others
the wind is the same; what differs is whether it meets a weak tree or a rock.
the commentary tells verses thirteen and fourteen about the Buddha's half-brother Nanda
he became a monk on his wedding day and pined for his bride before he settled.
Mara in the Dhammapada is the tempter who pulls people off the path
Müller adds '(the tempter)' after his name.

games.q: you're Nanda, newly a monk, and all you can think about is the bride you left behind. what does the story say happened?
o: he ran home and never came back.
with patience and practice, he thatched his roof.
games.why: the story says he struggled for a long time, then practiced steadily and became known for his self-control.

practice: Like someone walking around a house before the rains, look over your own roof: where does the weather get in?
Maybe the phone at night, hunger, tiredness, or one particular person who always gets under your skin; don't judge it, just find one weak spot and see it clearly.
Then ask, quietly, what one bundle of thatch could go there, an earlier bedtime, a snack before the hard meeting, and rest with that.

wordCard.voice: Ducchanna. Badly thatched: the same rain that leaks through a bad roof passes over a good one, as the same wind throws down a weak tree, not a mountain.

orig.note: Pali: badly covered, badly thatched, from verse thirteen.

carryVoice: Your line: thatch the roof. A bundle at a time, before the rains. Day one hundred sixty, done.

sources.q: will certainly overthrow him, as the wind throws down a weak tree.
than the wind throws down a rocky mountain.
As rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, passion will break through an unreflecting mind.
As rain does not break through a well-thatched house, passion will not break through a well-reflecting mind.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 9–12; Dhammapada-atthakatha, story of Nanda Thera (verses 13–14)
